Most marine scientists already fit models. You have written a GLM, checked residuals,
looked at a p-value, and drawn a conclusion about how temperature affects abundance.
So the obvious question about machine learning is: what is different?

The short answer is *what the model is for*. A statistical model is usually built to
tell you something about the world: the size of an effect, or whether it is
distinguishable from noise. A machine-learning model is usually built to make good
predictions about cases it has not seen. Those two goals pull in different directions,
and a model that excels at one can be useless at the other.

This section sets up that distinction and the vocabulary the rest of the course uses.
Every page works on the same simulated coastal survey, so you can see the same data
answer different questions.

## Further resources

**Documentation**

- [Get Started](https://www.tidymodels.org/start/), tidymodels. Five short articles that build one model from scratch, in the order this course uses.
- [Getting started](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/getting_started.html), scikit-learn. The same ground in one page, for readers who work in Python.
- [Choosing the right estimator](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/machine_learning_map.html), scikit-learn. A flowchart from the size and shape of your data to a method. Treat it as a starting point rather than an answer.
